--- title: "Testing the robustness of a published claim: the EU-frames case" author: "Pair: [names]" date: today format: html: toc: true toc-depth: 2 code-fold: false df-print: paged execute: message: false warning: false knitr: opts_chunk: fig-width: 8 fig-height: 5 --- ## The claim, and what we are doing to it The original author (OA) studied how citizens frame the European Union. One claim from their paper is our target: > "… poor economic performances … decrease positive dimensions of EU framing" (Teney 2016: 619) Operationalised the way that the Multi100 project constrained it for its five analysts: does a country's **unemployment rate** (poor economic performance) lower the **cosmopolitan** dimension of EU framing (peace, democracy, free movement, cultural diversity, a stronger say in the world)? The published result was a coefficient of −0.0034, t = −4.03. You have the data, the tools and the workflow that the project used, and the code you work through is the coordinator's own submitted analysis. You are analyst no. 6, and the question is how robust that number is to *justifiable* alternative choices. Work through the five tasks below in order, from a setup check to two dots on the live class chart – one explored, one declared. ::: callout-tip ## How the tasks work Every task is a callout box with instructions, a **TODO** you complete, and code chunks that **already run** – so the report renders from the first preview. You edit the prose blanks and, in Tasks 4 and 5, the code. The course site also has a browser version of this exercise, for practice without an installation or as a fallback if your machine fails; this workspace is the full IDE pipeline. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Task 1 – Set up, and fix the vocabulary"} **First, the setup check.** If this report renders at all, your workspace is working: the packages are installed, the data are in place, and the helpers are loaded. Render it once now, before anything else. If it does not render, run `source("R/check_setup.R")` in the console – it names the packages you are missing and how to install them. **Then, before touching data, fix the vocabulary.** In the four scenarios below, three are doing one of our three Rs, while one is doing something else entirely. **TODO: read the four scenarios and fill in the gaps.** ***Scenario 1:*** A reviewer reruns the authors' Stata `.do` file on the authors' data and gets a *different* coefficient from the one printed in the paper. This is an example of \_\_\_\_\_\_, even though what they *tried* to do failed. ***Scenario 2:*** The analyst uses the authors' submitted replication dataset, but they re-implement the model in R instead of Stata and centre the predictor. Is this a case of \_\_\_\_\_\_ or \_\_\_\_\_\_? ***Scenario 3:*** A preregistered team tests the identical hypothesis on a *separate, much larger* dataset chosen to be theoretically equivalent, and gets results that contradict the original. Their conclusion is that the original analysis has failed to \_\_\_\_\_\_. ***Scenario 4:*** Instead of the survey data used by the original authors, another researcher tests the same underlying idea on social-media texts using a machine-learning classifier method that the original never used. To their surprise, the authors' original findings prove \_\_\_\_\_\_ and the researcher concludes that they provide a reliable middle-range theory of the phenomenon they investigate. *(Answers: 1 reproducibility – the activity is reproducibility even though it failed to match, so the verdict is 'not reproduced'; 2 arguably still reproducibility, a grey area – re-implementing on the same data in different software is a re-computation, though centring the predictor and differing estimator implementations nudge towards robustness; 3 replicability – same question, independent new data; 4 generalisability – the impostor, new data and a new method at once.)* ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Task 2 – Meet the panel"} The **EU-frames dataset** (`EUframes_cy.csv`) is the country-year panel behind the whole exercise. It is already loaded as `euframes` in the setup chunk, and the copy in `data/` is byte-identical to the one published in the analyst's fork on OSF (osf.io/6zqct – "Multi100 \| Teney_EurSocioRev_2016 \| Analyst_C6HJR", main folder); the official Multi100 archival record is at osf.io/8rtwe. **TODO:** run the chunks, then read the small-multiples figure. Which countries trend down over 2004–2013? Note one in a comment. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # How many countries, how many years, how big is the panel? euframes |> summarise( countries = n_distinct(cntry), years = n_distinct(year), rows = n() ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: You should see **27 countries**, **10 years** (2004–2013), and **270 rows**. The outcome we care about first is `mcosmo` – the mean cosmopolitan framing of the EU in each country-year (a 0–1 scale). The predictor is `unemp`, the annual unemployment rate. The column `growth` is annual GDP growth, and `n_cy` counts the survey respondents behind each row. Every column is described in `data/EUframes_cy_codebook.md`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(euframes, aes(x = year, y = mcosmo)) + geom_line(colour = "grey55") + geom_point(size = 0.7) + facet_wrap(~ cntry, ncol = 6) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2004, 2008, 2013)) + labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean cosmopolitan framing (0–1)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Mean cosmopolitan EU framing over time, by country – a version of OA's Figure 1.](index_files/figure-html/fig-cosmo-trend-1.png){#fig-cosmo-trend width=864} ::: ::: Most countries drift gently; a few move sharply around the 2009 crisis. That variation within each country over time is what the fixed-effects model in Task 3 uses. *Downloading from OSF (optional).* `R/get_data.R` fetches this file from the analyst's OSF fork the way that a researcher would, with a course-site mirror as a fallback. It is not needed – the file already ships in `data/` – but running it gives you practice in downloading a published file from its repository: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Optional: confirm data/EUframes_cy.csv from OSF (uses the local copy offline). source("R/get_data.R") ``` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Task 2, continued – name the estimand, draw the graph"} Before estimating, say *precisely* what you are estimating. An estimand has two parts: a **unit-specific quantity** and a **target population** (Lundberg et al. 2021). State it outside any model. **TODO – complete the estimand statement:** > Unit-specific quantity: the change in \[\_\_\_\_\] for a one-point difference in \[\_\_\_\_\]. Target population: \[\_\_\_\_\]. *(A defensible filling: the change in mean cosmopolitan framing within a country-year, for a one-percentage-point difference in that country's unemployment rate; across EU member states, 2004–2013.)* Next come the identification assumptions: the claims about what causes what that must hold for the coefficient to be read as the effect of unemployment. `R/dag_starter.R` builds the graph with `dagify()`, where every arrow is an ordinary R formula written the way you read a regression, effect on the left of the tilde and cause on the right. `framing ~ unemployment` is therefore the arrow unemployment → framing. The causal path and the two confounder pairs are switched on; the arguable arrows are in the same call, commented out with a `#`, each with a line of justification above it. Open the file, take the `#` off any arrow you believe, re-source, and re-run `adjustmentSets()`. A node appears in the plot only once some arrow mentions it, so the plot shows only the graph that you have committed to. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} source("R/dag_starter.R") plot_dag(dag) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The starter DAG: unemployment → framing, with country and year as confounders.](index_files/figure-html/dag-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # What must we adjust for to identify the unemployment -> framing effect? dagitty::adjustmentSets(dag, exposure = "unemployment", outcome = "framing") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` { country, year } ``` ::: ::: For the starter graph the adjustment set is `{ country, year }`, which is what the two-way fixed effects that you fit in Task 3 absorb. Country fixed effects adjust for `country` and year fixed effects for `year`, so the DAG and the model encode the same identification claim. **TODO – answer two questions in a sentence each:** 1. What do **country** and **year** fixed effects adjust for, in plain terms? *(country-constant traits, and shocks common to all countries in a year)* 2. What can they **not** fix? *(a time-varying, country-level confounder – e.g. GDP growth moving both unemployment and framing within a country over time)* Whatever set is returned by your DAG becomes field 4 of the preregistration you write in Task 5. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Task 3 – Reproduce the recorded result"} This is the **reproducibility** check. Fit the two-way fixed-effects model that follows from the constraints of Task 2 in Multi100: cosmopolitan framing on grand-mean-centred unemployment, with country and year fixed effects. The target is **t = −3.804** (df = 233, N = 270) – the value on record for analyst C6HJR in the Multi100 dataset. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Grand-mean centre unemployment, as the submitted analysis did. With # two-way fixed effects this shifts the intercept, not the slope or the t – it # is the transformation that the constrained specification names, so do it # explicitly. euframes <- euframes |> mutate(unemp_c = unemp - mean(unemp, na.rm = TRUE)) # fixest::feols – the bar separates the regression from the fixed effects. m1 <- feols(mcosmo ~ unemp_c | cntry + year, data = euframes) tidy(m1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: {#tbl-corrected .cell tbl-cap='The constrained model on EUframes_cy.csv.'} ```{.r .cell-code} modelsummary( list("two-way FE (fixest)" = m1), estimate = "{estimate}", statistic = "t = {statistic}", gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared"), coef_rename = c("unemp_c" = "Unemployment (centred)") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
two-way FE (fixest)
Unemployment (centred) -0.003
t = -3.804
Num.Obs. 270
R2 0.754
``` ::: ::: The coefficient is **−0.00347** with **t = −3.804**, which is the value recorded for analyst C6HJR, reproduced from the published data and the published model. When two fixed-effect dimensions are present, `feols` reports classical (IID) standard errors by default, which assume that the errors are independent and identically distributed. That is why the *t* value matches, to three decimals, the value that the analyst obtained with `plm`. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Reproduction and the five analysts"} You reproduced the recorded value exactly, and so did everyone else in the class, because everyone ran the same code on the same file. That is why reproducibility is the cheapest of the three Rs to establish. The five Multi100 analysts each wrote their own code for the same claim, and came back with five different answers, one of them not significant. Their pipelines are competent, well-organised work, so the spread does not come from poor analysis. It arises because a claim stated in words leaves several defensible quantities open, and different analysts estimate different ones without noticing that they have chosen between them. In Task 2 you named the quantity you are after and drew the graph from which your adjustment set follows. In Task 4 you will see how far the answer moves when the other choices change. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Task 4 – Work the menu"} This task is **exploratory**. Try several specifications, see what each one does, and get a feel for which choices move the estimate and which barely touch it. Nothing here commits you to anything; the commitment comes in Task 5. `try_spec()` takes one argument per axis of the fourteen-axis specification menu. Every argument defaults to the baseline that you just reproduced, so changing one thing means changing one argument, and everything you do not name stays at the baseline. Every call is a real fit: the Level 1 arguments change the question, the Level 2 arguments select which version of the country-year panel is fitted (which items the outcome was built from, whether its cells were design-weighted, what was done with respondents who mentioned nothing, which published series supplies the predictor), and the Level 3 arguments set how the model is estimated. The one exception is the two imputed no-opinion options, whose pooled results are read from a shipped file because they need the respondent-level data that cannot be distributed with the workspace. The printed output notes when this happens. **TODO:** run the six calls below, then write your own. Print the log to see the small multiverse you have just built. Only the axes that you varied are shown, which keeps the comparison readable: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_experiments() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Specifications you have tried (7): outcome estimator sample weights noop measure b t r_aligned mcosmo fe_twoway all none zero wb_nat -0.00347 -3.80 -0.242 mpos fe_twoway all none zero wb_nat -0.00485 -4.99 -0.311 mcosmo pooled_cl all none zero wb_nat -0.00110 -1.04 -0.063 mcosmo fe_twoway no_bailout none zero wb_nat 0.00194 1.38 0.108 mcosmo fe_twoway all pop zero wb_nat -0.00300 -4.74 -0.296 mcosmo fe_twoway all none drop wb_nat -0.00466 -5.01 -0.312 mcosmo fe_twoway all none zero es_2064_pop -0.00431 -3.56 -0.227 sig TRUE TRUE FALSE FALSE TRUE TRUE TRUE Spread of claim-aligned r: -0.312 to 0.108 | significant: 5 of 7 ``` ::: ::: When you have tried three or four, decide which one you would defend if you had to, run it once more so it is the most recent, and submit it. It appears on the live class chart as an **exploratory** result: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} submit_exploration() ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why label it 'exploratory'?"} You chose this specification after seeing what several of them do, so it lacks the guarantee that a declared choice has: it might have been chosen *because* of its result, and neither you nor anyone else can now rule that out. Almost no published paper reports which of its analyses were explored and which were planned. The class chart does, because everyone submits twice: once here, and once in Task 5 after declaring, so the two sets of dots can be read against each other. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Task 5 – My preregistration"} Preregistration commits you to a choice **before** you see what it does, which stops you from quietly picking the specification that happens to give the answer you wanted. In this report the commitment is also enforced by the code. The session remembers the choices that you declare in the cell below, every later cell reads them from there, and the model builder refuses code that deviates from them. Make one choice on each of the fourteen axes of the specification menu, then run the cell. The seven Level 1 choices fix the question you are asking, the four Level 2 choices fix how that question is measured, and the three Level 3 choices fix how it is estimated. Every axis is live. `claim_align <- TRUE` is the course convention, applied automatically: negative framings are reverse-coded (1 − y) and the claim-expected sign for growth is flipped, so 'supports the claim' reads as a negative sign for everyone. Task 2 of Multi100 fixed unemployment as the measure on a gaussian scale; this menu lets you choose both. In Task 1 of Multi100, where the choice was left to them, four of the five analysts already used GDP growth, two of them beside unemployment. ::: ::: {.callout-important title="How this block maps to a real preregistration"} *A real preregistration, shortened. Each numbered comment maps to a question in the OSF "Preregistration Template from AsPredicted.org" (the eight-question short form). Because you are reanalysing data that already exist, field 2 also stands in for the prior-knowledge section of the secondary-data template (van den Akker et al. 2021) – the part that AsPredicted leaves out.* ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # ============================================================================ # MY PREREGISTRATION – one specification, declared before seeing its result # ============================================================================ # 1. The claim I am testing: ................................................. # 2. The data + what I already know: EUframes_cy.csv (270 country-years, # public); I know the constrained baseline gives t = -3.804. # 3. My one specification – one choice on each axis: # Level 1 – Estimands (each of these changes what is being estimated) my_outcome <- "mcosmo" # mcosmo | mutil | mpos (positive framings) # mcomm | mlib | mneg (negative framings) my_predictor <- "unemp" # unemp | growth (the measure that the claim is about) my_copredictor <- "none" # none | other (the other macro measure, adjusted for) my_estimator <- "fe_twoway" # fe_twoway | fe_country | re | pooled_cl my_sample <- "all" # all | y2004_2008 | y2009_2013 | no_bailout | no_GR_ES my_weights <- "none" # none | n_cell | n_eff | pop (re is never weighted) my_construction <- "share" # share | count | rate (share of own mentions, count of the # items in the set, or count per item in the set) # Level 2 – Measurement (the same question, put to the data differently) my_noop <- "zero" # zero | drop | split | mi_mice | mi_amelia # (respondents who mentioned no frame at all) my_item_set <- "all" # all | un (with or without the "unemployment" item) my_cell_weight <- "unweighted" # unweighted | design (cells as interviewed, or design-weighted) my_measure <- "wb_nat" # unemp: wb_nat | es_1574_act | es_2064_pop | es_2564_lfs | es_1574_tips # growth: wb_growth | es_growth # Level 3 – Estimation (the same question and measures, another fit) my_pred_form <- "raw" # raw | log (growth: raw only; centring or z-scaling # would leave t, r and p unchanged) my_family <- "gaussian" # gaussian | beta (logit link on the cell means; beta # reports z; standard measurement only) my_se <- "conventional" # conventional | clustered (clustered by country) claim_align <- TRUE # the course convention, applied automatically # 4. Why these controls, in one DAG-grounded sentence: ....................... # 5. Supported if the claim-aligned coefficient is negative and p < .05; # undermined if non-significant or positive. I will report what I get. prereg() # checks every choice against the menu and records the declaration ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` DECLARED – one specification, recorded before you see its result: The question (Level 1) outcome : mcosmo predictor : unemp adjusted : nothing estimator : two-way fixed effects (country + year) sample : all whose average: none scored as : share The measurement (Level 2) no-opinion rule: zero items: all cells: unweighted series: wb_nat The estimation (Level 3) form: raw family: gaussian errors: conventional claim_align: TRUE These choices are now fixed for the rest of the session, and the later cells read them from here. This rendered cell is your preregistration record, which timestamps the choice before you see its result. ``` ::: ::: An optional mirror form can be used to log preregistrations for the class, and the link to it is shared in the session. It is not required: the cell above, rendered into this report, is your official preregistration. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Task 5, continued – build, run and report"} This is the **robustness** check, and it is the part that your classmates cannot copy from you. Together, the class samples the multiverse of defensible analyses. You have declared your specification; now translate it into model syntax yourself. Fill the outcome, the right-hand side, and the estimator code exactly as you preregistered them. `build_model()` checks your code against your declaration and will not accept anything else; its error messages say what does not match. Write the log form as `log(unemp)`, and add any co-predictor with `+`. You do **not** write the fixed-effects, clustering, or family syntax here – the estimator and family codes stand for it, and `run_spec()` expands them into the real fit. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_model <- build_model(mcosmo ~ unemp, estimator = "fe_twoway") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Model accepted – it matches your preregistration: mcosmo ~ unemp, estimated by two-way fixed effects (country + year) Run it with run_spec(my_model). ``` ::: ::: When the model is accepted, run it. `run_spec()` fits your preregistered specification for real – the estimator, family, sample and weights expand into the matching `fixest`, `plm`, `betareg` or `glmmTMB` call, and the measurement choices select the version of the panel it is fitted on – and prints its claim-aligned result: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} run_spec(my_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Your preregistered specification, fitted live: mcosmo ~ unemp(raw) | fe_twoway | all | w:none [share, zero, items:all, cells:unweighted, wb_nat | gaussian, se:conventional] b = -0.00347 se = 0.00091 t = -3.804 on 233 df p < 0.001 claim-aligned partial r = -0.242 (below zero supports the claim) ``` ::: ::: Read the output like an analyst, looking at the coefficient and at its claim-aligned partial *r*, the correlation between predictor and outcome once the rest of the model is taken into account. A partial *r* below zero supports the claim. The five Multi100 analysts run from about the 16th percentile of the specification curve (the most strongly claim-supporting) to about the 68th (near the null), and your result is about to join theirs on the class chart. Now submit it to the class chart. There is nothing to fill in and nothing to transcribe – `report_result()` refits your declared specification, builds the spec label, and always submits on the claim-aligned scale that the chart is drawn on. It prints your submission line and a pre-filled form link; open it and press **Send**. Your dot appears on the live [Multiverse](https://codemoreh.github.io/applied-replication/results.html) chart within seconds, this time labelled **declared** rather than exploratory. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} report_result() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Your declared submission (claim-aligned, straight from your preregistration): spec: declared: mcosmo ~ unemp(raw) | fe_twoway | all | w:none [share, zero, items:all, cells:unweighted, wb_nat | gaussian, se:conventional] b = -0.00347 | se = 0.00091 | t = -3.804 | df = 233 | n = 270 | r = -0.242 Open the link below (or copy the URL) – the form opens with every field pre-filled; just press Send. https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSezoAEOnZUfP4pkfN28_XtEBwSyc2RLsXB-h8RPSegF7_t76A/viewform?usp=pp_url&entry.832496914=declared%3A%20mcosmo%20~%20unemp%28raw%29%20%7C%20fe_twoway%20%7C%20all%20%7C%20w%3Anone%20%5Bshare%2C%20zero%2C%20items%3Aall%2C%20cells%3Aunweighted%2C%20wb_nat%20%7C%20gaussian%2C%20se%3Aconventional%5D&entry.1656311800=-0.00347&entry.1337458262=0.00091&entry.1940779437=-3.804&entry.1682711955=233&entry.1586392724=270&entry.1660273001=-0.242 ``` ::: ::: If the form will not open on your machine, read the printed numbers to the facilitator and your dot will still be added. **A second declared specification?** Edit the preregistration cell, rerun `prereg()`, rebuild, rerun. The mechanics allow it, and the label does not change – so be clear with yourself about what the second one is. Your first declaration was made without knowing its result. Anything after it was not, which puts it back in the same category as Task 4, and you should say so when you report it. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Taking it home"} You did the whole analysis in a plain folder, with no version control and nothing to sign in to. Putting your own work under version control and publishing the rendered report to a live URL is the natural next step. A self-study module on the course site goes through it click by click: [Git and GitHub self-study](https://codemoreh.github.io/applied-replication/companion/git-github.html). The `.github/` and `.devcontainer/` folders already in this workspace set up that route once the folder is a repository again. ::: ::: {.callout-note title="Going further (optional)"} Each of these is a real fit that you can run in this workspace if you have time to spare. - **Sweep a whole axis.** `for (e in c("fe_twoway", "fe_country", "re", "pooled_cl")) try_spec(estimator = e)` fits all four estimators in one go, and `my_experiments()` then prints them side by side. The same trick works for any axis on the menu. - **The mirror-image expectation.** The claim is about *positive* framing. Preregister a **negative** dimension instead (`mneg`, or communitarian `mcomm`): if poor economic performance lowers positive framing, does it *raise* negative framing? With `claim_align <- TRUE` the reverse-coding (1 − y) is applied for you, so the result is reported on the same scale as the rest of the curve. - **Beyond unemployment.** Preregister `my_predictor <- "growth"` (GDP growth, which four of the five original analysts used when Multi100 left the choice of measure to them): the claim now predicts a *positive* growth coefficient on the positive framings, and the sign convention flips once more automatically. Refitted on the EU-frames panel, the model that analyst C6HJR chose in Task 1 of Multi100, `mpos ~ growth + unemp` with two-way fixed effects, gives a growth coefficient of b = +0.00167, t = 1.59, which is not significant. - **The full SCORE dossier.** OA's paper went through all three Rs in the SCORE programme and got three different verdicts: its push-button reproduction **failed** (the author-provided Stata code referenced file names that did not match what was available), its reproduction from the source data was recorded as **not reproduced**, and its preregistered secondary-data replication returned a **sign flip** (a positive coefficient, b = 0.002, p = .046, in the opposite direction to the original).
